items.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: the work “A Musical Tribute to Paul Robeson: When Sorrow Turns to Joy” that James Newton and I composed

ctx.x: As a parent, you are a parent and have a family, you have realistic living expenses and so forth, which part of your role as an artist helps you survive the most?

Well it’s different every year. In May, I think it was a May issue of Time magazine there was a list of occupations that had wage slashes and the top one was I think auctioneers. I think it was something like over 90 thousand to 45 thousand. And composers were the second, somewhere around 90 thousand to 45 thousand. So I mean yeah, this year it’s really slow. But you know in some ways artists, we’re able to deal with the fluidity of the economy. Especially people like me who improvise. I mean you improvise in the…

what’s a weakness in arts advocacy — because in some ways it’s been set up to be an entitlement program. And we’re just learning I think artists, arts makers, arts administrators, foundations and funders are just beginning to learn how do we articulate ourselves to be able to win people over, the public opinion. So and one way is how arts does, for every dollar that’s put in the arts, eight dollars is developed out of that. And arts helps build tourism, it creates other jobs with restaurants, hotels, taxicab…

items.title: Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2013
items.q: I’ll make a reference to Paul Robeson.

ctx.x: Did you say Melodies of China?

Melody. Melody of China. Which I’m not sure — I’ll make a reference to Paul Robeson. Because in the book Paul Robeson Speaks by Philip Foner, I think it’s on Beacon Hill Press back in the 1970’s, before Robeson passed. He was performing at Swarthmore College giving a lecture demonstration before that term was invented, because he’d always speak and frame the songs he was singing, which was the musics of the world, not just European tradition but also what he calls the Negro spirituals, I’d rename it the…
